summary: The error-handling and core logging plumbing is genuinely solid: the global HttpExceptionFilter never leaks stack traces, SQL, internal ids, or file paths to clients (5xx are re-skinned to a generic message + random supportCode; the full trace is logged server-side on one greppable line), and there is no NODE_ENV-gated verbose error path. main.ts and worker.ts both install unhandledRejection/uncaughtException handlers that log loudly and exit non-zero (worker drains first), so the process never dies silently or zombies. Graceful shutdown via enableShutdownHooks + a 25s worker drain deadline is in place. /metrics is genuinely not publicly reachable — Caddy 404s /metrics, /healthz, /readyz on both the public and admin /lbr-api/* paths, the API container publishes no host ports (internal docker network only), and metric labels are aggregate-only (tenant counts by status, capacity gauges) with no per-tenant slug/id PII. The EXP-001 export error path correctly runs redactSecrets() before persisting pg_dump failures to the tenant-visible job.error field, and control-plane exports redact password hashes / MFA secrets / DB-role secrets / tokens via redactRow. Pino does not log request bodies (so login/signup passwords aren't captured) and redacts Authorization + Cookie headers. The two prior audits' "ready" verdict on plumbing largely holds. What they MISSED is on the accountability/PII-at-rest side: the most material gap is that sensitive Libriant-staff and billing mutations write NO durable audit row despite a purpose-built audit_log table existing, and Stripe webhook payloads (customer PII) are stored and exported unredacted. These are HIGH/MEDIUM gaps, not plumbing bugs.

findings.title: Sensitive admin & billing mutations write no audit_log row (revenue/entitlement changes are untraceable)
findings.evidence: The control-plane AuditEvent model (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:878, @@map("audit_log")) exists precisely for this — it has actorType/actorId/action/beforeJson/afterJson/ip/userAgent and even documents `subscription.changed` as an example action (line 884). But `auditEvent.create` is called in only 3 places (admin-tenants.controller.ts:204 tenant hard-delete, tenant-audit.service.ts:48, platform-settings/admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:42). billing.service.ts:379-380 comments `audit happen exactly once per state change`, yet applyAdminPlanChange() (l.388) and applyManualPayment() (l.410) just do `controlDb.subscription.update(...)` with NO audit write. Confirmed via grep: admin-overrides, admin-plans, and admin-system-mode controllers contain zero `auditEvent`/`audit`/`logger.` references. So a Libriant operator (or a compromised admin session) can grant a tenant a free paid plan, extend paidUntil indefinitely, flip platform-wide pricing, toggle feature overrides, or trigger a global maintenance/out_of_order takeover with no durable, queryable record of who/when/before/after.
findings.impact: No forensic trail for revenue-affecting and platform-wide control actions performed by staff. Defeats insider-abuse detection, fraud investigation (manual paid-until grants), incident reconstruction (who took the fleet down), and any SOC2/GDPR accountability claim. The only trace is the ephemeral pino access log (method+path, no actor identity, no before/after, rotated).
findings.fix: Write an auditEvent.create row (actorType=ADMIN, actorId=admin.sub, ip from client-ip, userAgent, before/after snapshots) in each of these handlers/service methods, mirroring admin-tenants.controller.ts:204. Use actions like subscription.changed, subscription.paid_until_set, plan.updated, feature_override.set, system_mode.set. The schema is already there; only the writes are missing.

adversarial.reason: Partially confirmed but materially overstated. CONFIRMED: the control-plane AuditEvent model exists with all claimed fields and even documents `subscription.changed` (packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:878-901), yet only 3 production `auditEvent.create` call sites exist (admin-tenants.controller.ts:204, tenant-audit.service.ts:48, admin-subscriptions.controller.ts:42). billing.service.ts:388-431 applyAdminPlanChange/applyManualPayment do a bare `controlDb.subscription.update(...)` with no audit write, and the Subscription model (schema:464-495) has NO actor/history field at all — so admin plan grants and paidUntil extensions are genuinely untraceable (who/when/before). admin-plans.controller.ts:116-138 plan price/feature edits overwrite Plan in place with no audit row either. That billing/plan surface is a real, legitimate observability gap. OVERSTATED / REFUTED in part: the claim's headline impact ("trigger a global maintenance/out_of_order takeover... with no durable record" and "feature overrides... no record") is wrong. SystemModeEvent (schema:965-982) has a REQUIRED createdByAdminId with a Restrict relation, set at admin-system-mode.controller.ts:112/133 (createdByAdminId: admin.sub), plus startsAt/endsAt/mode/createdAt and a /history endpoint — so "who took the fleet down" IS durably and queryably recorded. TenantPlanOverride (schema:439-455) carries createdByAdminId set at admin-overrides.controller.ts:106 with note/expiresAt — override creation is attributed on the row itself (the DELETE at :121 is the only unattributed override action). SEVERITY: this is a forensics/observability concern, not RCE/auth-bypass/cross-tenant/data-loss. Every cited handler is gated by AdminAuthGuard + AdminRolesGuard + @AdminRoles('owner') (owner-only platform staff); the threat model is insider abuse / incident reconstruction, not an external exploit on the running product, and pino access logs capture method/path/timing. Given two of the three asserted surfaces already have per-row attribution, the real blast radius is narrower than the high rating claims. Real and worth fixing for the subscription/plan billing surface, but medium, not high.

findings.title: Stripe webhook payloads (customer PII) stored unredacted and shipped in control-plane exports
findings.evidence: stripe-webhook.controller.ts:79 persists the FULL event: `payloadJson: event as never` into stripe_webhook_events.payloadJson (schema.prisma:654 `payloadJson Json`, retained ~30d). For invoice.payment_* and customer.subscription.* events the raw Stripe body contains customer PII — customer_email, customer_name, customer_address/billing_details, and card brand/last4. The control-plane export redactor (export-processors.ts redactRow → isSensitive, l.61-66) only matches column NAMES against /token|secret|passwordhash|password_hash/ or the explicit SENSITIVE_COLUMNS map (l.52-57). The column `payloadjson` matches none of these, so readTables (l.390) emits it verbatim. A control/all-scope CSV/JSON/XLSX export therefore writes customer emails, names and billing addresses into an unencrypted file retained 24h on the shared storage volume.
findings.impact: Customer PII at rest in webhook table and exfiltrated into unencrypted export artifacts. GDPR data-minimisation / right-to-erasure exposure and a juicy target if the storage volume or an export download link leaks. Exports are admin-only (mitigating), but the file persists outside auth and the PII is broader than needed for replay.
findings.fix: Either (a) store a slimmed payload (drop customer email/name/address/payment-method details, keep ids + amounts needed for replay), or (b) add `stripe_webhook_events: new Set(['payloadjson'])` to SENSITIVE_COLUMNS so control-plane exports redact it. Also add stripe_webhook_events.error if it can ever carry PII. Set/verify a TTL prune job actually runs (schema says 30d).

findings.title: /metrics relies solely on Caddy + network topology (no in-app guard) — leaks fleet-wide tenant counts if either layer regresses
findings.evidence: HealthController is `@Controller()` with no @UseGuards; @Get('metrics') (l.61) returns libriant_tenants_total{status}, libriant_storage_used_bytes, pg connection/cache gauges, redis memory — i.e. whole-fleet operational intelligence. The ONLY protection is Caddy `respond @internal 404` for /metrics on the public and admin /lbr-api/* routes (Caddyfile:149,196) plus the api container publishing no host ports. There is no second layer at the app: any process on the shared `app` docker network (e.g. the web container, or a future side-car) can GET http://api:3001/metrics directly and read fleet tenant counts. A single Caddyfile edit/regression silently re-exposes it.
findings.impact: Defense-in-depth gap. Aggregate-only (no per-tenant PII in labels), so impact is limited to leaking total tenant/capacity counts, but it's a single-layer control on data that should be operator-only.
findings.fix: Add a lightweight in-app guard on /metrics (shared-secret bearer token the Prometheus scrape config carries, or bind metrics to a separate internal-only listener). Keeps the Caddy 404 as belt, adds braces.

findings.title: redactSecrets() leaks part of a DB password that contains an '@' character
findings.evidence: redactSecrets = s.replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/[^:@/\s]+:)[^@/\s]+@/gi, '$1***@'). The password class [^@/\s]+ stops at the first '@'. Tested: input `pg_dump postgresql://tenant_role:S3cr3tP@ss@db:5432/...` → output `postgresql://tenant_role:***@ss@db:5432/...`, leaking the `ss` tail of the password into the tenant-visible exportJob.error field. Generated DB-role secrets are normally @-free (hex/base64url), so this only bites if a password (e.g. an operator-set superuser password in a connection URL) contains '@'.
findings.impact: Partial credential disclosure into the tenant-readable job.error field, but only for passwords containing '@' (uncommon for generated secrets; possible for operator-chosen superuser creds). Low real-world likelihood.
findings.fix: Anchor to the last '@' before host or strip the whole userinfo: e.g. replace(/(postgres(?:ql)?:\/\/)[^@\s]*@/gi, '$1***@') so the entire user:pass segment is masked regardless of '@' in the password.

findings.title: export-worker logs raw err.message (possibly an unredacted connection string) to operator stdout
findings.evidence: `worker.on('failed', (job, err) => console.error(`[export-worker] job ${job?.id} failed: ${err.message}`))`. The export-processors path redacts secrets before persisting to the DB (job.error), but this BullMQ failure handler logs the raw err.message to stderr/container logs. A pg_dump/connection failure message can include `postgresql://user:pass@host`, so a tenant DB credential could land unredacted in operator-visible container logs (not tenant-visible).
findings.impact: Operator-only log exposure of a tenant/superuser DB credential on export failure. Container logs are access-controlled, so impact is limited to log-aggregation surface.
findings.fix: Run the existing redactSecrets() over err.message in the worker failed handlers (export-worker.ts:41 and similar in import/email/maintenance workers) before logging.
